newsitem.title: USA: Cosmetics shopping -- function over fashion.
newsitem.headline: Cosmetics shopping -- function over fashion.

text.p: Cosmetics companies believe they are in the business of creating style, but a retail consultant says they are digging their own graves by not paying attention to what consumers really want.

"New season cosmetics colour statements are no longer relevant to consumers who don't change their 'look' each season," said Wendy Liebmann, president of WSL Strategic Retail, a New York City-based marketing and retail consulting company.

"What cosmetics companies don't seem to understand is that if they are not careful they risk going the way of the apparel business. Consumers do not need another gray eye shadow or red lipstick, just as they have little need for another traditional work outfit, with the casual trend continuing to grow," she said.
Overall, cosmetics sales have been flat for the past three years and Liebmann predicted that this will continue "until marketers realise that consumers have changed their attitudes toward beauty."
Today, cosmetics are viewed by most women as a functional commodity, "no longer an image-driven category." This, Liebmann believes, "is not a good sign for cosmetics retailing in the new millennium."

According to the survey, "How America Shops," conducted by WSL earlier this year, overall, cosmetics sales have declined by 1 percent from last year. Hair and skin care products have, by contrast, risen 8 percent and 6 percent, respectively.
"Over the past five years, sales of cosmetics, hair care and skin care (products) have been highly resistant to economic shifts as consumers view these products almost like staples," Liebmann said.

WSL's research indicates that the majority of consumers are loyal to a particular brand and most likely will buy it in a department store if they are upper income ($70,000 plus annual salary). Lower-to-middle income women ($12,000 to $44,000) are more likely to shop mass merchandisers.

Mass merchandisers, drug and department stores dominate the skin care/cosmetics categories. The WLS survey showed that the majority of consumers have stable shopping habits both in brand loyalty and retail loyalty.
Because of this double-barrelled loyalty, cosmetics shoppers don't necessarily "shop sales," Liebmann said. "Consumers search for the lowest everyday prices..."

There is expected to be growth, however, in moderate-to-lower priced lines, as consumers choose to spend $5 on a lipstick rather than $15 on the identical one next door. Celebrity spokeswomen are already representing the moderate priced lines, showing that high price and celebrity status need not go hand in hand.

At a time when shoppers are buying less cosmetics, they are also buying 28 percent less jewellery and 8 percent fewer home decorating products. On the other end of the scale, the WSL survey showed, consumers are buying 21 percent more food and 13 percent more clothing.
